meta.title: Who really said "If a poem hasn't ripped apart your soul, you haven't experienced poetry"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Edgar Allan Poe. Quote Investigator traces the line to a 2014 tweet from a Twitter account named @Edgar_Allan_Poe, and the Poe Museum rejects it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If a poem hasn't ripped apart your soul, you haven't experienced poetry'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Poe: the line goes back to a May 2014 tweet by a Twitter account called @Edgar_Allan_Poe. Quote Investigator and the Poe Museum both reject the Poe credit.

answer.label: Not Edgar Allan Poe — a 2014 tweet
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence that Poe wrote or said this line. Its chronology starts with a tweet posted on 7 May 2014 by a Twitter account called “@Edgar_Allan_Poe,” and it concludes that the person running that account probably wrote it. Readers then assumed the account’s name meant the famous author had written it, which QI calls “naming confusion.”

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Poe Museum, “Did Poe Really Say That?” (10 Sep 2014)

source.excerpt: If a poem hasn’t ripped apart your soul; you haven’t experienced poetry.
trail: 7 May 2014 — The Twitter account @Edgar_Allan_Poe tweets the line. Quote Investigator reports that the tweet had more than 1,300 likes and more than 1,400 retweets by June 2021 (Quote Investigator ↗).
May 2014 — The line spreads on Tumblr credited to “Edgar Allan Poe.” A tweet dated 7 May 2014 carries it back to Twitter with the same credit (Quote Investigator ↗).
10 Sep 2014 — The Poe Museum’s blog post “Did Poe Really Say That?” by Chris Semtner says: “I am firmly putting my foot down when I say Poe did not say this” (The Poe Blog ↗).
12 Jun 2021 — Quote Investigator concludes that the link to the nineteenth-century Poe is spurious (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: Wording of the 7 May 2014 tweet, as transcribed by Quote Investigator. The tweet uses a semicolon. The version usually passed around uses a comma.

author.name: Unidentified Twitter account (@Edgar_Allan_Poe)
author.heading: About the @Edgar_Allan_Poe Twitter account
author.metaLine: Social-media account using Poe's name · active 2014
author.bio: A Twitter account with the handle @Edgar_Allan_Poe and the display name “Edgar Allan Poe.” Quote Investigator says the person behind the account probably wrote this line, and the sources do not identify that person. The real Edgar Allan Poe (1809–1849) was an American poet, short-story writer and critic. He could not have posted to a social network.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Poe
misattribution.intro: The line is credited to Edgar Allan Poe on quote sites and social media. The trail leads to a Twitter account that uses his name, not to anything Poe wrote.

items.why: Quote Investigator found “no substantive evidence” that Poe, who died in 1849, wrote or said it. QI traces the credit to a tweet from the account @Edgar_Allan_Poe (Quote Investigator ↗).

Chris Semtner’s 2014 post lists the line among quotes falsely credited to Poe: “Just because it appears on popular media sites like Tumblr and Pinterest doesn’t mean it is an authentic quote” (The Poe Blog ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The line goes back to a May 2014 tweet by the Twitter account @Edgar_Allan_Poe. The account’s name led readers to credit the poet (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: How a handle becomes a byline
lead: Quote Investigator calls this mechanism “naming confusion.” A Twitter account named after a famous writer posts a line. Readers who see the name assume the writer said it, then share it with that credit. Tumblr reblogs and quote-aggregator pages copy the credit again, and nobody checks it against Poe’s actual writings.
The Poe Museum lists this line among more than twenty sayings it says Poe never wrote, or that are distorted versions of real Poe passages. Its curator’s verdict is blunt: “Poe did not say this.”
context.pull: “I am firmly putting my foot down when I say Poe did not say this.” — Chris Semtner, The Poe Museum
